Ready to build a practical, command-line-first workflow for network troubleshooting?

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Network Performance
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Network Performance Monitoring and Analysis

Learn the core metrics and a command-line toolkit to monitor, diagnose, and troubleshoot network issues on Linux servers.

In this lesson

Collect interface counters, inspect sockets, watch live bandwidth, and run controlled throughput tests to isolate network vs application problems.

Why it matters

Networks underlie every connection between services. Accurate measurement prevents wasted effort chasing the wrong layer.

Visual summary
Metrics
Bandwidth, throughput, latency, packet loss
Tools
ip, ss, netstat, sar, iftop, ping, traceroute, iperf3
Troubleshooting
Physical checks, traffic observation, throughput testing, kernel and NIC tuning
Explore Key Topics
Core metrics
Learn what each metric reveals about traffic and user experience.
CLI toolkit
Practical commands to inspect interfaces, sockets, and live bandwidth.
Diagnosis flow
A repeatable sequence to move from symptom to root cause.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the hands-on skills you will practice. First, you will be able to interpret core network metrics: bandwidth describes the maximum possible rate, throughput is what you actually observe, latency is round-trip delay, and packet loss is when packets fail to reach their destination. A practical example: a 1 Gbps link with frequent packet loss will often show low throughput despite high bandwidth. Second, you will use inspection tools to examine sockets and interfaces. Commands like ss and ip show listening sockets and interface counters so you can spot high connection counts or rising error counters. Third, you will monitor traffic in real time with sar and iftop, learning to identify top talkers and per-second rates. Fourth, you will run connectivity and capacity tests with ping, traceroute, and iperf3 to separate network-path problems from application issues. Each objective maps to a small demonstration and a verification milestone so you can prove your competency. As you progress, remember the common misconception: advertised link speed is not the same as usable throughput — counters and tests tell the real story.

screens.title: Bandwidth, Throughput, Latency, Packet Loss
screens.narratorSegment: Begin with clear definitions, because misreading terms wastes time. Bandwidth is a link's maximum theoretical transfer rate, often the number advertised for an interface such as 1 Gbps. Throughput is the actual data rate you achieve during a transfer; throughput is what your users experience and it is typically lower than bandwidth due to protocol overhead, congestion, and retransmits. Latency is the time it takes for a packet to travel to a destination and back when measuring round-trip; high latency makes interactive apps feel sluggish even when throughput is high. Packet loss is when packets fail to reach their destination; loss triggers retransmissions, which both increases effective latency and reduces throughput. A concrete example: two hosts separated by a long, lossy link may show high bandwidth on their NICs but very low throughput—many packets retransmit, and connection throughput is constrained by the TCP window and loss rate. A common misconception is to equate advertised bandwidth with usable bandwidth; always measure throughput under realistic conditions. Key takeaway: know which metric answers which question — capacity, user rate, responsiveness, or reliability — so you pick the right diagnostic tool.

keyIdea.title: Metric mapping
keyIdea.text: Choose the metric that corresponds to the user symptom: slow transfers → throughput, laggy interaction → latency, incomplete data → packet loss.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Metrics
Definitions
Bandwidth
Maximum theoretical data rate of a link, e.g., 1 Gbps.
Throughput
Actual data rate observed during transfers; affected by overhead and loss.
Latency
Time delay for packets; high latency degrades responsiveness.
Packet loss
Packets not delivered; causes retransmits, higher latency, and lower throughput.
Analogy
Think of bandwidth as the width of a pipe, throughput as the water you get out, latency as the delay before water arrives, and packet loss as holes in the pipe that leak water.
Example & Misconception
Concrete example
# Link advertises 1 Gbps, iperf3 shows 200 Mbps
iperf3 -c 10.0.0.2 -t 10
If iperf3 shows 200 Mbps despite a 1 Gbps NIC, investigate loss, latency, and device errors rather than assuming the NIC is broken.
Key Takeaway

Measure throughput and counters to confirm whether a perceived capacity issue is actually bandwidth, loss, or latency-driven.

screens.title: Inspect connections with netstat, ss, and ip
screens.narratorSegment: Inspection is your first step when you suspect a network problem. Netstat is a legacy but familiar command to list sockets, routes, and interface statistics; examples include listing listening ports with process names. The modern replacement, ss, does the same job faster and scales better when there are many connections. Use ss -tulnp to show TCP and UDP listeners with associated PIDs. Meanwhile, ip provides interface configuration and counters; ip addr show lists addresses, and ip -s link show eth0 prints bytes, packets, errors, and drops for the interface. A concrete workflow: if users complain about connection failures, run ss -tulnp to check that the expected service is listening. If a service is listening but clients fail, run ip -s link show to look for rising errors or drops on the interface. A common misconception is treating a listening port as proof of reachability — listening is necessary but not sufficient; you must verify interface state and routing. In practice, combine socket inspection with interface counters and a quick ping to confirm end-to-end reachability before deep-diving into application logs. What does your socket list tell you about who is bound to each port?

keyIdea.title: Inspect first
keyIdea.text: Confirm services are listening and interfaces are healthy before assuming the problem is in application code.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Inspect Tools
Command examples
netstat
netstat -tulnp  # TCP/UDP listening ports with PID/program name
netstat -s       # Summary statistics for all protocols
ss
ss -tulnp  # Faster socket listing
ss -s      # Summary statistics
ip
ip addr show
ip -s link show eth0  # bytes, packets, errors, dropped
Explanation & example
Scenario

Users report a service connection error. Run ss -tulnp to verify the process is listening, then ip -s link show to check for interface errors. If the interface shows RX errors, start with physical checks like cables and switch ports.

Common mistake

Assuming a listening port means reachability. Always verify interface health and routing as well.

Key Takeaway

Combine socket listings with interface counters to build a reliable hypothesis about reachability.

screens.title: Using ip -s link and ethtool for interface health
screens.narratorSegment: Interface counters are strong diagnostic evidence. The ip -s link show command reports bytes and packet counts plus RX errors and TX errors for each interface; sustained errors are often physical or driver-related. For example, rising rxerr/s suggests receive-side problems which may result from a bad cable, duplex mismatch, or a faulty switch port. ethtool complements ip by revealing NIC settings, speed, duplex, and offloading configuration; ethtool -S shows detailed driver statistics. A practical check: if ip -s link show eth0 reports a high receive error count but transmit errors are zero, suspect the physical medium or switch on the far side rather than your server's transmit ability. A misconception is to immediately change offload settings or drivers — while offloading can impact behavior, start with cable and port checks, then confirm settings with ethtool. Use repeated ip -s samples or sar -n EDEV for trends rather than a single snapshot. Your takeaway: interface counters point you to the likely layer and reduce wasted changes to higher-level configuration. Using ip -s link and ethtool for interface health means rx/tx error patterns help you determine whether to start at the physical layer, nic driver, or upstream switch.. In practical terms, interpret rx/tx errors, dropped packets, and nic statistics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: RX/TX error patterns help you determine whether to start at the physical layer, NIC driver, or upstream switch.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Interface Health
ip -s link show
ip -s link show eth0
# shows: RX packets, RX errors, RX dropped, TX packets, TX errors, TX dropped
Interpretation
  • High RX errors → likely receive-side physical issue or duplex mismatch.
  • High dropped packets → buffer drops, possible congestion or driver limits.
  • Compare TX and RX patterns to localize upstream vs server problems.
ethtool for NIC details
ethtool eth0        # show speed, duplex, offload
ethtool -S eth0     # detailed NIC statistics
Practical example

If RX errors climb and ethtool shows a mismatch in duplex or lower negotiated speed, check the switch port and cable. Duplex mismatch often causes collisions and receive errors.

Key Takeaway

Use ip counters and ethtool together to identify whether a problem is physical, driver, or configuration related.

screens.title: Monitoring with sar -n and iftop
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring has two complementary needs: short-term, live inspection and longer-term sampling for trends. sar -n DEV provides per-interface statistics at regular intervals, including bytes and packets per second; running sar -n DEV 1 5 samples every second for five samples to show short bursts. sar -n EDEV reports error statistics for devices so you can detect rxerr/s and txerr/s trends. iftop provides a live, interactive view of bandwidth per host or connection and is excellent for finding top talkers during a spike. A practical workflow: when a spike occurs, start sar -n DEV in the background to record sampling over minutes while you open iftop to see which remote hosts consume the link now. Remember that iftop requires root to see per-connection traffic on an interface and may need installation. A common misconception is relying solely on iftop's interactive snapshot; always pair it with sar samples or logs to confirm whether the observed usage is sustained. Your objective is to correlate a top-talker found by iftop with traffic counts recorded by sar to decide whether the spike is transient, scheduled, or caused by misuse.

keyIdea.title: Pair live and historical
keyIdea.text: Use iftop to find immediate top talkers and sar to confirm patterns over time and capture error trends.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Monitoring
Tools
sar -n DEV / sar -n EDEV and iftop
Live → Trend
sar examples
sar -n DEV 1 5    # network device stats every 1s, 5 times
sar -n EDEV 1 5   # error stats for devices
Use sar to capture short sampling windows or longer collections for post-analysis.
iftop
sudo iftop -i eth0   # interactive per-connection bandwidth monitor
iftop shows which remote hosts consume bandwidth at the moment you run it.
Example workflow

Start sar to sample every second, then run iftop to see current top talkers. Correlate the iftop snapshot with sar samples to decide if the spike is sustained.

Key Takeaway

Short interactive views and repeating samples together give both context and evidence for remediation decisions.

screens.title: Using ping and traceroute to map latency and path
screens.narratorSegment: Ping and traceroute are inexpensive, immediate ways to test reachability and observe latency along the path. Use ping with a small count to test round-trip time and packet loss; persistent packet loss reported by ping is usually a sign of network path issues that need deeper investigation. Traceroute lists each hop between you and the destination and reports per-hop latency; increased latency at a particular hop helps locate where delays occur. A typical workflow is: first ping the destination to confirm basic connectivity and measure round-trip time and loss; if you see high latency or loss, run traceroute to determine which intermediate hop introduces the delay. Be aware of a misconception: an individual hop showing high latency does not always mean that hop is the true culprit — some routers deprioritize ICMP or TTL-expired responses. Another practical detail: when diagnosing routes to remote services, traceroute can reveal asymmetrical routing or unexpected detours that increase latency. Close your test with a reflective question: does high latency trace to a single hop or is it accumulated across several hops? That answer directs you to the network operator responsible for the problematic segment.

keyIdea.title: Localize with traces
keyIdea.text: Ping confirms reachability and loss; traceroute helps pinpoint the hop where latency or routing detours begin.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › Connectivity
ping — simple reachability
ping -c 5 google.com  # send 5 packets and report RTT and loss
If ping shows packet loss or high RTT, that is evidence of network issues affecting responsiveness.
traceroute — path and per-hop latency
traceroute google.com  # shows each hop and latency to that hop
Look for the first hop where latency jumps or responses fail; that narrows the responsible network segment.
Misconception

Some routers deprioritize ICMP or TTL-expired responses, so a slow traceroute hop is a clue, not absolute proof. Correlate with application traces and other tests.

Key Takeaway

Use ping first to confirm reachability, then traceroute to find where delays arise; always corroborate traceroute clues with other evidence.

screens.title: Measuring capacity with iperf3
screens.narratorSegment: iperf3 is the controlled experiment you run when you need to know network capacity between two hosts. It requires an iperf3 server process on one host and an iperf3 client on the other. Start the server with iperf3 -s, then run the client with iperf3 -c -t 10 to test for 10 seconds. Using parallel streams with -P can reveal whether a single TCP stream or the path limits throughput; for example, iperf3 -c -t 10 -P 5 starts five parallel streams. A common use-case: if your application is slow but iperf3 shows near-advertised throughput, the bottleneck is likely internal to the server or the application stack, not the network path. Conversely, if iperf3 shows low throughput, you must investigate the network path, interface errors, or intermediate devices. A misconception is to trust a single short test — repeat tests at different times and compare to interface counters and sar samples to ensure the result is consistent. In short, iperf3 separates capacity questions from application-level performance questions, giving you a decisive test to guide next steps. Measuring capacity with iperf3 means use iperf3 to measure raw tcp/udp capacity between hosts and compare results to interface counters to locate the bottleneck layer.. In practical terms, controlled client/server tests to separate network from application bottlenecks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Controlled testing
keyIdea.text: Use iperf3 to measure raw TCP/UDP capacity between hosts and compare results to interface counters to locate the bottleneck layer.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.5 › iperf3
Setup
# Server
iperf3 -s

# Client
iperf3 -c 10.0.0.2 -t 10         # 10 second test
iperf3 -c 10.0.0.2 -t 10 -P 5    # 5 parallel streams
Compare iperf3 output to your interface's advertised speed and ip -s counters to draw conclusions.
Example diagnosis
Scenario

If iperf3 measures near 900 Mbps on a 1 Gbps link, the network path is likely fine. If your web app is still slow, investigate CPU, memory, disk I/O, or application design.

Common mistake

Interpreting a single short iperf3 run as definitive. Repeat tests and correlate with sar or ip counters for robust conclusions.

Key Takeaway

iperf3 gives a controlled throughput baseline that helps you decide whether to troubleshoot the network or the application.

screens.title: Common network bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring themes when networks underperform. Start by understanding these common bottlenecks and their typical evidence. Insufficient bandwidth occurs when the link cannot carry the traffic volume; you will see sustained high utilization on sar or iftop. High latency arises from long distances, congested routers, or poor wireless links and is visible with ping and traceroute. Packet loss destabilizes throughput; repeated retransmissions show up as decreased iperf throughput and packet loss in ping. Network interface errors indicate problems with cables, NICs, drivers, or duplex settings and appear as RX/TX errors in ip -s link show or sar -n EDEV. Firewall or security rules can block or delay traffic; check rules if connections are unexpectedly refused or timed out. TCP-specific limitations such as TCP window size may limit throughput on high-latency, high-bandwidth paths, while NIC offloading issues can cause unexpected behavior and are diagnosable with ethtool -k and ethtool -S. A misconception is assuming a single root cause; in practice multiple layers can interact. Prioritize inspection by collecting counters and running iperf3 to determine whether the problem is within the network path or beyond it.

High latency arises from long distances, congested routers, or poor wireless links and is visible with ping and traceroute. Packet loss destabilizes throughput; repeated retransmissions show up as decreased iperf throughput and packet loss in ping. Network interface errors indicate problems with cables, NICs, drivers, or duplex settings and appear as RX/TX errors in ip -s link show or sar -n EDEV. Firewall or security rules can block or delay traffic; check rules if connections are unexpectedly refused or timed out. TCP-specific limitations such as TCP window size may limit throughput on high-latency, high-bandwidth paths, while NIC offloading issues can cause unexpected behavior and are diagnosable with ethtool -k and ethtool -S. A misconception is assuming a single root cause; in practice multiple layers can interact. Prioritize inspection by collecting counters and running iperf3 to determine whether the problem is within the network path or beyond it.

screens.title: A repeatable troubleshooting sequence
screens.narratorSegment: A disciplined, repeatable flow saves time and prevents unnecessary changes. Start at the physical layer: verify cables, link lights, and switch port status when interface errors or packet loss appear. Next, test connectivity and latency with ping and traceroute to determine path and hop-level delays. Then monitor traffic with iftop or sar -n DEV to identify heavy users or unusual patterns. Use iperf3 to measure raw throughput between two hosts and differentiate network capacity from application-level issues. Check firewall rules and connection tracking if packets are being dropped or connections terminated. Examine kernel network parameters using sysctl to adjust backlog and timeout settings only after you confirm they are relevant to the symptom. Finally, review NIC settings with ethtool for duplex and offload options. A concrete example: on seeing high RX errors, first check cables and switch ports, then run ethtool to confirm negotiated speed and duplex, then correlate with sar samples for traffic patterns. A misconception is jumping to sysctl changes before gathering clear evidence; follow the flow and change one item at a time while measuring the effect.

Check cables, link lights, and switch ports for errors.

Ping and traceroute to local and remote hops.

screens.title: Examine and tune kernel network parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Kernel network parameters can influence connection backlog, timeouts, and reuse behavior and are worth inspecting when you're dealing with high connection rates or specific TCP issues. Use sysctl -a | grep net. to explore available settings. A useful quick action is adjusting net. core. somaxconn, which controls the maximum backlog for listening sockets; raising it can help heavily loaded servers accept bursts of new connections more gracefully. Example: sudo sysctl -w net. core. somaxconn=65535 changes the running kernel parameter; for persistence add the setting to /etc/sysctl. conf. However, a misconception is to treat sysctl changes as universal fixes — many parameters address specific scenarios and may have side effects. Always measure before and after a change and prefer incremental adjustments with validation under realistic load. If you find socket backlog or TIME-WAIT issues, combine sysctl checks with ss and application tuning to ensure you are addressing the real bottleneck, not masking symptoms of resource exhaustion or inefficient application handling. Examine and tune kernel network parameters means change sysctl settings only when evidence points to a kernel-level limit; measure the impact under load and persist changes intentionally.. # example: view somaxconn

Example change

screens.title: NIC offloads and ethtool troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: NIC offloading features like checksum offload, TSO, and LRO are designed to improve performance by moving work into hardware. In many environments these features increase throughput and reduce C P U, but sometimes drivers or hardware have bugs or interactions that cause incorrect behavior or measurement discrepancies. Use ethtool -k eth0 to inspect offload settings and ethtool -S eth0 to view NIC statistics. If you suspect offload-related problems, you can temporarily disable a specific offload and retest to see if behavior changes. For example, turning off large receive offload may be useful when debugging checksum or packet reassembly anomalies. A common misconception is to disable offloading by default — in most cases offloading improves performance and should be enabled unless evidence shows otherwise. Always combine ethtool checks with ip -s counters and repeat iperf3 tests after toggling settings to confirm whether the change helps. Your final takeaway: use offload toggles as controlled experiments, not permanent blind fixes. In practical terms, when offloading helps and when it can cause problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
Network performance shapes how users experience your services. In this lesson you will learn the fundamental metrics — bandwidth, throughput, latency, and packet loss — and the practical command-line tools to measure and diagnose them. You will see how lightweight commands like ip and ss reveal interface and socket state, how sar and iftop let you watch traffic over time, and how ping, traceroute, and iperf3 isolate connectivity and capacity issues. We'll also cover common bottlenecks and an ordered troubleshooting approach so you can move from symptom to cause. For example, running an iperf3 test between two hosts can show whether the path can sustain expected throughput; if iperf3 is healthy but your application is slow, the problem likely lives inside the server or app. Keep in mind a common misconception: high advertised bandwidth doesn't guarantee high throughput — real traffic is shaped by latency, packet loss, and device errors. By the end of the module you'll be able to collect reliable evidence, interpret interface counters, and choose the right next diagnostic command. Ready to build a practical, command-line-first workflow for network troubleshooting?

These objectives guide the hands-on skills you will practice. First, you will be able to interpret core network metrics: bandwidth describes the maximum possible rate, throughput is what you actually observe, latency is round-trip delay, and packet loss is when packets fail to reach their destination. A practical example: a 1 Gbps link with frequent packet loss will often show low throughput despite high bandwidth. Second, you will use inspection tools to examine sockets and interfaces. Commands like ss and ip show listening sockets and interface counters so you can spot high connection counts or rising error counters. Third, you will monitor traffic in real time with sar and iftop, learning to identify top talkers and per-second rates. Fourth, you will run connectivity and capacity tests with ping, traceroute, and iperf3 to separate network-path problems from application issues. Each objective maps to a small demonstration and a verification milestone so you can prove your competency. As you progress, remember the common misconception: advertised link speed is not the same as usable throughput — counters and tests tell the real story.

This second objectives slide shows how you will practice, what to measure, and a simple verification for each skill. For metrics, practice by measuring a link with iperf3 and correlating that output to interface counters from ip -s link show; a successful verification is consistent throughput with low errors and no packet loss. For inspection tools, run ss -tulnp and ip addr show to find stray listeners and unexpected addresses; verify by mapping a PID to a service and confirming expected ports are bound. For live monitoring, run sar -n DEV at short intervals and an iftop session; verification is identifying the top talkers during a load spike. For diagnostics and troubleshooting, stage an iperf3 server and run client tests, then use ping and traceroute to local hops to isolate latency; verify by reproducing the symptom and showing which layer changed when you remedied it. A common misconception to avoid: running a single short test rarely proves stability — use repeated samples and correlate counters to build confidence in your diagnosis.

Begin with clear definitions, because misreading terms wastes time. Bandwidth is a link's maximum theoretical transfer rate, often the number advertised for an interface such as 1 Gbps. Throughput is the actual data rate you achieve during a transfer; throughput is what your users experience and it is typically lower than bandwidth due to protocol overhead, congestion, and retransmits. Latency is the time it takes for a packet to travel to a destination and back when measuring round-trip; high latency makes interactive apps feel sluggish even when throughput is high. Packet loss is when packets fail to reach their destination; loss triggers retransmissions, which both increases effective latency and reduces throughput. A concrete example: two hosts separated by a long, lossy link may show high bandwidth on their NICs but very low throughput—many packets retransmit, and connection throughput is constrained by the TCP window and loss rate. A common misconception is to equate advertised bandwidth with usable bandwidth; always measure throughput under realistic conditions. Key takeaway: know which metric answers which question — capacity, user rate, responsiveness, or reliability — so you pick the right diagnostic tool.

Inspection is your first step when you suspect a network problem. Netstat is a legacy but familiar command to list sockets, routes, and interface statistics; examples include listing listening ports with process names. The modern replacement, ss, does the same job faster and scales better when there are many connections. Use ss -tulnp to show TCP and UDP listeners with associated PIDs. Meanwhile, ip provides interface configuration and counters; ip addr show lists addresses, and ip -s link show eth0 prints bytes, packets, errors, and drops for the interface. A concrete workflow: if users complain about connection failures, run ss -tulnp to check that the expected service is listening. If a service is listening but clients fail, run ip -s link show to look for rising errors or drops on the interface. A common misconception is treating a listening port as proof of reachability — listening is necessary but not sufficient; you must verify interface state and routing. In practice, combine socket inspection with interface counters and a quick ping to confirm end-to-end reachability before deep-diving into application logs. What does your socket list tell you about who is bound to each port?

Interface counters are strong diagnostic evidence. The ip -s link show command reports bytes and packet counts plus RX errors and TX errors for each interface; sustained errors are often physical or driver-related. For example, rising rxerr/s suggests receive-side problems which may result from a bad cable, duplex mismatch, or a faulty switch port. ethtool complements ip by revealing NIC settings, speed, duplex, and offloading configuration; ethtool -S shows detailed driver statistics. A practical check: if ip -s link show eth0 reports a high receive error count but transmit errors are zero, suspect the physical medium or switch on the far side rather than your server's transmit ability. A misconception is to immediately change offload settings or drivers — while offloading can impact behavior, start with cable and port checks, then confirm settings with ethtool. Use repeated ip -s samples or sar -n EDEV for trends rather than a single snapshot. Your takeaway: interface counters point you to the likely layer and reduce wasted changes to higher-level configuration. Using ip -s link and ethtool for interface health means rx/tx error patterns help you determine whether to start at the physical layer, nic driver, or upstream switch.. In practical terms, interpret rx/tx errors, dropped packets, and nic statistics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Monitoring has two complementary needs: short-term, live inspection and longer-term sampling for trends. sar -n DEV provides per-interface statistics at regular intervals, including bytes and packets per second; running sar -n DEV 1 5 samples every second for five samples to show short bursts. sar -n EDEV reports error statistics for devices so you can detect rxerr/s and txerr/s trends. iftop provides a live, interactive view of bandwidth per host or connection and is excellent for finding top talkers during a spike. Your objective is to correlate a top-talker found by iftop with traffic counts recorded by sar to decide whether the spike is transient, scheduled, or caused by misuse.

Ping and traceroute are inexpensive, immediate ways to test reachability and observe latency along the path. Use ping with a small count to test round-trip time and packet loss; persistent packet loss reported by ping is usually a sign of network path issues that need deeper investigation. Close your test with a reflective question: does high latency trace to a single hop or is it accumulated across several hops? That answer directs you to the network operator responsible for the problematic segment.

These final concept cards capture the practical commands and heuristics you will use often. ss or netstat let you inspect active sockets and listeners; ip gives interface addresses and counters. sar -n DEV and iftop are complementary: sar captures sampled device stats over time, while iftop shows live per-connection bandwidth. Ping and traceroute help localize latency and routing issues; iperf3 provides controlled throughput measurements between two hosts. As a troubleshooting heuristic, always follow the physical-to-application flow: verify hardware and link status, confirm path and latency, measure capacity with controlled tests, and only then tune kernel or NIC settings with tools like sysctl and ethtool.
